title: In The Line of Fire (1993), is probably John Malkovich’s best role, as well as an incredibly realistic and underrated thriller.

commenti.body: Sure it’s a solid performance from Malkovich but overall the movie has definitely got the Eastwood style all over it. Did a binge on his 80s 90s thrillers and they all have a similar vibe to them.

Damn, what is up with the repackaging of the word “underrated?” I totally agree with tour writeup, but this movie is in no way underrated. This is a classic flick. Here are the stats:


*Literally a 96% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes.


*Directed by Wolfgang Peterson with an absolutely stacked cast for the time, including Gary Cole and John Mahoney.


*$187m gross against a $40m budget. Absolute runaway success at the box office.


*Three Academy Award noms for Malkovich, screenplay writer Jeff Maguire, and editor Anne Coates.


*Parodied in Mad Magazine back when it still had relevance, implying that it had reached at least a minimal threshold of being relevant to the zeitgeist of the time.


Dude, I totally agree that it’s a great movie, but in no way could this be considered underrated. This is a classic flick that is popularly and critically well-regarded.

Fantastic film. It’s arguably one of the best thrillers in the last 30 years. It’s a rare thriller where the conversation scenes are engrossing as the action scenes. The violence is brutal & the climax is incredibly exciting.

I disagree with two things. First, Eastwood was wonderful. He’s subtle but he serves as a superb balance to Malkovich’s empowering (but brilliant) performance.

Second, I don’t think he killed the hunters because of the bird. Yes, he may give that implication, but I would argue it was actually because he told them he was going to kill the President. He wasn’t necessarily someone whose comments should be taken at face value.

I get what bro is saying, though. "Underrated" wasn't a good word for it.

How would you feel about "underappreciated today"? I think it definitely is, the movie doesn't come up much in conversations about 90s movies. 

We definitely tend to forget some excellent thrillers from that golden age that I think kinda hold up today. Off the top of my head: The Long Kiss Goodnight, Conspiracy Theory and The Pelican Brief.

Eastwood was good, but I still think John steals the show.

Malkovich did kill them for the reasons you state, but he was disgusted with their petty act when he himself had such a grand target.

‘Eastwood was good, but I still think John steals the show.’

Oh, I definitely agree that Malkovich was the best. I just think that Eastwood was better than you described. 

‘Malkovich did kill them for the reasons you state, but he was disgusted with their petty act when he himself had such a grand target.’

I think that’s a great way of looking at it.

“Underappreciated today” is absolutely fair. Especially if applied in the context of younger viewers who may not have been exposed to this kind of film. 

The other movies you mentioned are definitely contemporaries or successors. The thriller genre thrived and matured through the 90’s, the decade ending with Fight Club, for example. But it all started getting really amped up in the mid-late 80’s. Movies like The Firm, Mississippi Burning, etc. 

Such a freaking bounty of beautiful thrillers during this time. I know I was being pedantic in my last post but if anyone here is looking for a thriller recommendation from this era, please reach out.

> Leary shows a certain level of honour and has his own moral standards (he kills two hunters for shooting a bird) and the violence he does depict (murdering two women because one of them could have blown his cover story) is horrifyingly plausible.

Sorry, but those two hunters were dead the second they spoke to him. He didn't kill them because of a duck, he killed them beacuse they were loose ends.

I think the point of the two guys killing a... sitting duck, was to prove, through metaphor, that these two hunters were themselves sitting ducks. A brilliant brilliant scene. I remember the movie pleasure of knowing OH THEY ARE FUCKED when they talked to Malk.
That vibe is good though. True Crime and Absolute Power do have that same vibe, but they don't rise to the level of In The Line of Fire.

Someone smarter than me noted there are parallels between this film and what is perhaps one of Eastwood’s best known films, *Dirty Harry*.

The *general* plot is the same: Lawman pursuing psychopath who taunts him and tries to upend the system.

But the tone is changed and having an older Eastwood we have him doing things differently than the younger version of himself as Harry Callahan.

I think it makes for an interesting contrast to see the films back to back!
